analysis.one_liner: Bans the largest, most anticompetitive corporate mergers and lets regulators unwind past ones.
analysis.headline: The bill won support from 13 House Democrats but never received a committee vote or floor action, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban certain large mergers outright: any deal over $5 billion, any deal that would give the buyer more than a third of a product market or a quarter of a job market, and deals that push market concentration past set limits. It would also let the FTC and the Justice Department reject mergers directly, rather than having to win a lawsuit, and would let them retroactively break up deals since 2000 that left a company with over half a market. State attorneys general could sue to block mergers too, and the FTC and DOJ would each get $1 billion a year in funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, small businesses, and farmers. The bill treats monopsony power — a few employers dominating a local job market — as a merger problem, so the ban on buying more than a quarter of a labor market is aimed at raising wages. Consumers in markets like health care, groceries, and telecom would face fewer price-raising consolidations, and the bill targets harms to small and minority-owned businesses, rural communities, and communities of color.

how_it_helps.text: Bans mergers over $5 billion, mergers giving the buyer over 33% of a product market or over 25% of a labor market as an employer, and deals that push the Herfindahl-Hirschman concentration index past set thresholds [S2, S3].
Lets the FTC and DOJ reject acquisitions directly as an agency decision, ending the current system where agencies must win a federal court case to stop a merger [S2, S3].
Requires the FTC and DOJ to review and potentially unwind mergers consummated since 2000 that left a firm with over 50% of a market or otherwise materially harmed competition [S2, S3].

Lets state attorneys general sue to block mergers and gives the NLRB, SBA Office of Advocacy, and Minority Business Development Agency formal grounds to object to deals that would harm workers, small businesses, or minority-owned firms [S3].
Authorizes $1 billion a year each for the FTC and the DOJ Antitrust Division, whose merger-review workload the bill's findings say has overwhelmed current staffing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations that want to acquire competitors, private equity and asset-management funds that profit from serial acquisitions, investment banks and law firms that earn fees on mega-deals, and shareholders of dominant firms whose consolidation strategies — including buying up nascent competitors and rolling up local markets — would be blocked or reversed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big merger parties and private equity

drawbacks.text: The bright-line rules ban any deal above $5 billion regardless of its competitive effects, and courts reviewing agency rejections may not weigh any procompetitive benefits against anticompetitive harms, so even genuinely efficient mergers could be blocked with no offsetting defense [S3].

The bill strips the Supreme Court of appellate jurisdiction over antitrust decisions under the bill and channels all appeals to the D.C. Circuit, a structure that would face serious constitutional challenge [S3].

Mandatory 120-day review periods, extensive disclosure requirements (executive compensation histories, data assets, trade secrets, ten largest customers and suppliers), and CEO personal liability for false filings would add substantial compliance cost and delay for any deal above $50 million involving large firms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core case is strong: research cited in the bill's own findings links four decades of consolidation to higher prices, lower wages, brittle supply chains, and the collapse of startup rates, and the current agency-run merger system has approved most large deals. The blunt bright-line bans and the prohibition on weighing merger efficiencies are a real cost — some large deals genuinely do lower prices or rescue failing firms, and the failing-firm defense in the bill is narrow. But the bill preserves judicial review of agency rejections, so the main objections are about design aggressiveness, not a lack of consumer benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, sent to their subcommittees, and never received a markup, a committee vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Mondaire Jones introduced the bill on March 16, 2022, with 11 original cosponsors, and 13 House Democrats cosponsored it in total; no Republican did [S3, S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].

It was sent to the Consumer Protection and Commerce subcommittee on March 17, 2022, and to the Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law subcommittee on November 1, 2022; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died at the end of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations, private equity funds, and dominant platforms that would have faced an outright merger ban and retroactive unwinding are better off because the bill never advanced. So are the investment banks and law firms that collect fees on mega-mergers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations and private equity funds

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported it; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists, and it sat without action in committees chaired by Democrats for the rest of the Congress.

industries.industry: Large corporations pursuing mergers (firms with $5B+ revenue)
industries.note: Deals above $5 billion, deals above a 33% market share, and rollups of labor markets would be banned outright, and deals since 2000 that left a firm with over half a market could be unwound. The bill exists to stop exactly what these firms have spent decades doing.

Funds with $10 billion or more under management would face mandatory merger filings, retroactive review of nonreportable deals, and disqualification from acquisitions if they have paid antitrust settlements or faced antitrust findings in the prior decade. Serial acquisition is the core of the private equity model.

The bill specifically targets acquiring a nascent competitor or maverick and creates a category for platform conflicts of interest — owning a platform while competing on it — any of which could trigger rejection or unwinding. The largest acquisitions by large platforms are typically of young competitors.

Longer 120-day review windows, heavier filing requirements, CEO personal liability, and an outright ban on the largest deals would shrink deal volume and fees. Their revenue comes from transactions the bill restricts.

industries.industry: Small businesses, farms, and minority-owned firms
industries.note: The bill gives the SBA Office of Advocacy and the Minority Business Development Agency formal standing to object to mergers that would materially harm them, and cites rollups of farms, retail, and local services as core harms. Small suppliers and independent retailers compete against consolidated buyers and sellers.
